lines.text: Gus is trying to open a plane door seven miles up, and he's in no danger at all.
It's three in the afternoon, he just woke up from a nap, and he thinks it's the bathroom.
His wife screams. His neighbor grabs his seat belt.
Gus pulls harder. Nothing. He puts a foot on the wall. Still nothing.
But wait. Gus isn't that weak. So what's holding the door shut?
You see, up here the air outside is thin. It presses a fifth as hard as the air on the ground.
So the cabin is pumped up like a tire, and all that air wants out.
It leans on every square inch of the door, eight pounds harder than the thin air outside pushes back.
And a door has a lot of square inches. Add them up, and you get almost twenty thousand pounds.
That is the weight of four cars, parked on the door.
Ever pull a suction cup off a window? There's no glue. It's just air pushing on one side.
A plane door is a plug, a bit bigger than its hole, so it has to come in before it swings out.
To open it, Gus would have to drag in all four cars.
Unluckily, he still needs the bathroom, and the door only lets go on the ground.
So he tries the next door, the one door on this plane he can open.
